findings.title: Failed work is still marked complete
findings.body: The `finally` block marks every item’s offset complete, including when `result_processor` raises and the worker logs the exception. The commit loop can then commit past a result that was never processed, preventing Kafka from redelivering it. The normal `ResultProcessor` also catches handler exceptions and returns, so those failures likewise appear successful to this tracker. Only mark an offset complete when processing has actually succeeded, or explicitly define and test a skip-on-error policy.

findings.title: The work queues are unbounded
findings.body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to an unlimited size, so `put()` does not provide the natural backpressure claimed by this implementation. If Kafka delivers faster than the workers can process, queued `WorkItem`s accumulate in memory until the consumer process can be OOM-killed. Bound the queues and ensure a full queue appropriately slows or pauses consumption.

findings.title: Shutdown exits workers without draining queued work
findings.body: Setting `worker.shutdown` before shutting down the queues makes each worker exit after its current item; `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` does not override the loop condition or ensure the remaining items are processed. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close` also stops the commit thread before shutting down the pool. Pending items therefore remain unprocessed and uncommitted at shutdown, causing them to be replayed after restart and potentially duplicating side effects. Drain the queues and allow completed offsets to be committed before stopping the workers and commit thread.

findings.title: Shutdown relies on a Python 3.13-only queue API
findings.body: `Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were added in Python 3.13. On supported runtimes below 3.13, this call raises `AttributeError`, which is swallowed here; workers blocked in `get()` are never woken, and each `join(timeout=5.0)` leaves daemon worker threads behind. Use a shutdown mechanism supported by the project’s Python versions, or explicitly require Python 3.13+.

findings.title: A negative worker count silently drops results
findings.body: The CLI accepts any integer for `--max-workers`, and a negative value is truthy here, so it is passed as `num_queues`. `range(num_queues)` then creates no queues or workers. Submissions fail when indexing the empty queue list, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that failure and marks the message offset complete, allowing it to be committed without processing. Reject non-positive worker counts before starting the consumer.
